author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the 3D structural components of DNA: two antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones, four nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A–T with 2 H-bonds; G–C with 3 H-bonds) to determine sequence relationships across the helix.
Explain antiparallel orientation and how sugar-phosphate directionality enforces 5'→3' vs 3'→5' running.
Trace DNA replication at the replication fork by matching enzymes (helicase, SSBs, DNA polymerase, DNA ligase) to their roles.
Describe why leading synthesis is continuous and lagging synthesis is discontinuous into Okazaki fragments based on DNA polymerase’s 5'→3' building rule on antiparallel templates.
Predict daughter-molecule composition after one and two rounds of semiconservative replication.

modules.description: Begin with a schematic ladder showing sugar-phosphate backbones, base-pair rungs, and base identity in a clear, non-geometric representation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish backbone segments from base-pair rungs in a ladder schematic.
Recognize A, T, G, C base identity labeling and how pairing occurs across the ladder.
Interpret hydrogen-bond counts as a proxy for base-pair stability.
instructions: Center the ladder in your workspace (~1 arm length from you).
Watch the rungs appear; focus on how each colored base segment meets in the middle.

components.text: DNA ladder: rails = sugar-phosphate backbones; rungs = base pairs (A–T, G–C)

clips.changeMeaning: The schematic DNA ladder is instantiated and made visible as the starting representation, keeping the workspace uncluttered so students can first map backbone vs base-pair structure. The text legend anchors the learner’s attention to the key parts (rails and rungs).
clips.narration: Welcome! This first scene uses a simple DNA ladder to reveal the repeating backbone and the base pairs that connect them.

clips.changeMeaning: Colored rungs for adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine appear in the ladder’s interior. This sets up complementary pairing identification before bond-count emphasis.
clips.narration: Each rung contains two bases—color coding helps you see adenine paired with thymine, and guanine paired with cytosine.

modules.description: Transform the ladder into a realistic double helix and introduce a toggle to switch between schematic and helix representations during the same scene.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Connect ladder schematic features to the corresponding 3D double-helix geometry.
Describe the approximate helical periodicity (one full turn ~10 base pairs).
Observe groove-like surface features as emergent geometry.
instructions: Use the toggle to switch between ladder and helix.
Rotate the model to see backbones spiraling around a shared axis.

clips.changeMeaning: Helix and ladder are staged in the same location so learners can match the schematic rails/rungs to the 3D geometry before focusing on twisting behavior.
clips.narration: Now we move from a ladder representation to the actual double-helix geometry—two intertwined backbones with base pairs stacked between them.

clips.changeMeaning: The helix performs a one-turn twist animation to communicate helical periodicity. Base stacking remains visible so learners associate ladder rungs with interior stacking along the helix.
clips.narration: Watch how the structure spirals. A full turn is roughly every ten base pairs.

modules.description: Show arrows on both sugar-phosphate backbones to establish antiparallel orientation and label each strand’s 5' and 3' termini.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify antiparallel orientation: one strand runs 5'→3' while the other runs 3'→5'.
Interpret 5' and 3' labels as termini of the sugar-phosphate backbone directionality.
Use rotation to confirm arrow directions from different viewpoints.
instructions: Rotate the helix to verify the arrows.
Read the 5' and 3' labels at both ends of the two strands.

clips.changeMeaning: The arrow bundle appears on top of the helix, explicitly showing that the two backbones run in opposite directions. This isolates the key conceptual variable: directionality.
clips.narration: Next, let’s make antiparallel orientation explicit. One backbone runs 5' to 3', while the other runs 3' to 5'.

clips.changeMeaning: Terminal labels are emphasized so learners can connect each 5'/3' tag to the correct strand end. With rotation enabled on the helix, students can confirm the antiparallel relationship from any viewing angle.
clips.narration: These 5' and 3' labels mark the ends of each sugar-phosphate backbone.
